clue.text: He crusaded with 1 down, 5, 9, 12, 17, 18, 20, 22 and 24

blocks.note: surface reading: a medieval king who went on crusade
setter's reading: the first name shared by every person in the listed entries

explanation.surface: A crusader king rides out alongside a whole company of named companions.
explanation.walkthrough: RICHARD the Lionheart led the Third Crusade; the cross-references are the puzzle's theme, all famous Richards: Rodgers, Hakluyt, Dawkins, Adams, Hoggart, Branson, Strauss, Grant and Nixon.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard I of England was a crusading monarch, and every themed surname in the grid belongs to a famous bearer of this forename.

clue.text: Expressions of agreement about Dutch collaborator in South Pacific

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the first word wraps round the second

blocks.note: 'Roger!' is radio slang for 'understood, agreed'
standard abbreviation for Dutch

explanation.surface: Someone nods along to a Dutch partner working on a project in the South Seas.
explanation.walkthrough: South Pacific is a musical, not a place here: Richard Rodgers wrote its music with Hammerstein's lyrics.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Rodgers composed the score of the musical South Pacific in partnership with lyricist Oscar Hammerstein.

clue.text: Buckaroo's Brahmin bonnet

blocks.note: Brahmin (Brahman) is a breed of humped cattle
a poke bonnet is a woman's bonnet with a projecting brim

explanation.surface: A cowboy's headgear is described as fit for a Hindu priest.
explanation.walkthrough: Brahmin looks like the Hindu caste, but here it is the cattle breed. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Buckaroo and cowpoke are both American slang words for a cowboy who herds cattle on the range.

clue.text: March maid accepts it in friendship

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it inside, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: Amy March is the youngest sister in Little Women
taken as written

explanation.surface: A young woman marching takes something in a spirit of friendship.
explanation.walkthrough: March is not the month or a walk but the family name of the sisters in Louisa May Alcott's Little Women.
explanation.definitionFit: Amity is a formal word for peaceful, friendly relations between people or nations.

clue.text: Demonises characters in state capital

indicators.note: the word is broken into its characters, its letters, to be laid out anew

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone vilifies the inhabitants of a capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: Characters reads as people being demonised; here it means letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Des Moines is the capital city of the US state of Iowa.

clue.text: Geographer saying: "Cut and can it"

indicators.note: saying means the words are spoken, and their sound gives the spelling of a name

blocks.note: to hack is to cut roughly
can and loo are both slang for a lavatory
taken as written, then run into the previous sound

explanation.surface: A geographer's motto: cut it out and put it in a tin.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken quickly, hack-loo-it approximates the surname, usually said HACK-loot. Can is US slang for the toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Hakluyt was an Elizabethan writer who compiled accounts of English voyages and promoted geographical knowledge.

clue.text: Can't stand English bowlers around?

indicators.note: around means placed on every side, so the hats enclose the letter

blocks.note: bowlers are hard round hats
standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A cricket fan cannot bear to have English bowlers nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: Bowlers sound like cricketers; they are the hats.
explanation.definitionFit: To hate something is to be unable to stand or tolerate it, so the verb phrase matches.

clue.text: Make Peter sadly attend all the lectures

indicators.note: sadly suggests things have gone badly wrong, so the letters are thrown out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sadly forces a student called Peter to go to every lecture.
explanation.walkthrough: Make looks like the verb of compulsion; it is part of the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: At old universities and the Inns of Court, to keep a term was to satisfy residence and attendance requirements for that period.

clue.text: Argue wildly about doctor with spleen that is taken

indicators.note: acting wildly means without order, so these letters are scrambled
about means surrounding, so the scrambled word goes round the abbreviation

blocks.note: taken as written
MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's degree

explanation.surface: A patient argues angrily with a doctor about a diseased spleen being removed.
explanation.walkthrough: The spleen sounds like the organ a doctor would take out, but it means bad temper, and 'that is taken' points to the idiom 'take umbrage'.
explanation.definitionFit: Umbrage is resentment or offence, and spleen is an old word for ill humour; one proverbially takes umbrage.

clue.text: Ancient staff rights in your old country

indicators.note: in places one item inside the gap between the other two

blocks.note: thy is the archaic form of your
R is right, so two of them make rights
the United States

explanation.surface: A historian discusses the rights people enjoyed in the old country.
explanation.definitionFit: A thyrsus was the ivy-wreathed staff carried by Dionysus and his followers in ancient Greece.

clue.text: Atheistic zoologist was kind to solvers

indicators.note: handed to solvers, the words become a puzzle whose letters they must rearrange

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A famously combative atheist scientist was, for once, gentle with crossword solvers.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal is unusual: the letters are simply given to the solver to work on.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Dawkins is an evolutionary biologist and prominent atheist, author of The Selfish Gene and The God Delusion.

clue.text: Aspen shaking head of bog myrtle

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter
shaking jumbles things up, so these letters are reordered

blocks.note: first letter of bog
taken as written

explanation.surface: An aspen tree quivers beside bog myrtle, as if a nature guide described two plants.
explanation.walkthrough: Aspen reads as the tree, but it is used as an adjective: aspen leaves are proverbial for quivering.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective aspen means quivering or tremulous, like the leaves of that poplar, which is what trembly means.

clue.text: 'pon my soul! 'e left out poor Tom Jones, for example

indicators.note: something left out is omitted, so that letter is dropped from the mix
poor suggests something in bad shape, so the remaining letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, a dropped-aitch he
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for left, and it is removed

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned exclamation at someone omitting Fielding's poor hero Tom Jones.
explanation.walkthrough: Left does double duty in the surface, but only 'out' with it signals removal of L. Tom Jones is the hero of Fielding's novel of the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: An eponymous character gives his name to the work he appears in, as Tom Jones does to Fielding's novel.

clue.text: Modern writing includes a literary anthropomorphist

indicators.note: to include is to hold within, so the article goes inside

blocks.note: AD, the Christian era, as opposed to BC
MS is a manuscript
taken as written

explanation.surface: Contemporary fiction finds room for a writer who gives animals human traits.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Adams wrote Watership Down, whose rabbits talk and think like people.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Adams gave rabbits human speech and society in Watership Down, which is literary anthropomorphism.

clue.text: Generator's output in revs per minute

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit inside the run of following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and into the next two

explanation.surface: A technical note on an electrical generator's output measured against engine speed.
explanation.walkthrough: Generator sounds like an engine; here it is a male parent.
explanation.definitionFit: Sperm is the reproductive output of a male, the one who generates offspring, a jokey sense of generator.

clue.text: Might his KO stymie new contenders?

definitions.text: Might his KO stymie new contenders?

indicators.note: might hints at what the letters could become if rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A sports writer wonders whether a champion's knockout punch will deter fresh challengers.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the boxer, while its middle words supply the letters. The anagram signal is loose: 'Might' asks what those letters might make.
explanation.definitionFit: Mike Tyson was a heavyweight boxing champion whose knockout power frightened off many would-be challengers.

clue.text: Splitting heads with the French eminence

indicators.note: splitting something opens a gap in it, and the article fills that gap

blocks.note: two words for head: nob, slang for a head, and ness, a headland
French for the

explanation.surface: Splitting heads sounds like a violent French encounter.
explanation.walkthrough: Heads gives two different words, the slang nob and the headland ness, and the French article goes between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Eminence means high rank or distinction, as nobleness means exalted station or character.

clue.text: Flea bit you twice, say? Bad as Foster's dreamer!

indicators.note: say tells us to listen to how the phrase is spoken

blocks.note: bitten again and again, you are bit-you-full, full of bites

explanation.surface: A flea has bitten someone repeatedly, and it is likened to a song about a dreamer.
explanation.walkthrough: Stephen Foster wrote the song 'Beautiful Dreamer'. Bad is slang for excellent, so the description is ironic praise.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen Foster's song is addressed to a Beautiful Dreamer, and bad in slang means great or attractive.

clue.text: A-bomb survivor: his cry of surprise rings round Azerbaijan's capital

indicators.note: to ring round something is to encircle it, so these letters surround the city

blocks.note: taken as written
ha is an exclamation of surprise
Baku is the capital of Azerbaijan

explanation.surface: A survivor of the atomic bomb shouts in surprise while circling a Caspian city.
explanation.walkthrough: Azerbaijan's capital tempts you to take its first letter; here it is the whole city name.
explanation.definitionFit: Hibakusha is the Japanese term for survivors of the 1945 atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

clue.text: Skill of the Ettrick Shepherd? His literacy had its uses

blocks.note: the poet James Hogg was known as the Ettrick Shepherd
art is a skill

explanation.surface: A shepherd's skill is praised because his ability to read paid off.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the first part backwards: the Ettrick Shepherd's skill. Richard Hoggart wrote 'The Uses of Literacy'.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Hoggart's best-known book is The Uses of Literacy, a 1957 study of working-class culture.

clue.text: Creator of "Virgin and Child" (after British artist and knight)

indicators.note: after means coming behind, so the child is placed at the end

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for British
RA, Royal Academician
N is a knight in chess notation
a son is a child

explanation.surface: An old master painting of the Madonna and Child is attributed to an English painter.
explanation.walkthrough: Virgin and Child looks like a painting's title; split it: Virgin is the business brand, and Child is wordplay. Richard Branson founded the Virgin group.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Richard Branson founded the Virgin brand, from records to airlines, so he is its creator.

clue.text: Cult figure when observed during the day

indicators.note: something seen during a period is set within it, so one word is placed inside the other

blocks.note: Mon, Monday
as can mean when, as in 'as he left'

explanation.surface: A cult member is spotted in broad daylight.
explanation.walkthrough: Cult is a teasing description of Freemasonry, with its secret rites.
explanation.definitionFit: A Mason is a member of the Freemasons, a secretive fraternal society that the clue jokingly calls a cult.

clue.text: Was his Danube as blue as his Levis?

definitions.text: Was his Danube as blue as his Levis?

blocks.clueFragment: Was his Danube as blue as his Levis?
blocks.note: surface reading: one man's river compared with his blue jeans
setter's reading: two different men share a surname, the waltz composer and the jeans maker

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a man's river was as blue as his denim jeans.
explanation.walkthrough: Johann wrote the Blue Danube waltz, and Levi founded the jeans firm; the theme's Richard of that name composed operas.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname belongs to Johann the waltz king, Levi the denim maker and Richard the opera composer.

clue.text: But Ophelia didn't get here in order to obey Hamlet

definitions.text: But Ophelia didn't get here in order to obey Hamlet

blocks.note: surface reading: a place Ophelia never reached
setter's reading: Hamlet told her 'Get thee to' this place, a religious house where she would be in holy orders

explanation.surface: Ophelia ignored Hamlet's instruction about where to go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In order' also hints at a religious order. Ophelia drowned rather than follow Hamlet's famous command.
explanation.definitionFit: A nunnery is a convent of nuns, the place Hamlet harshly tells Ophelia to go in Shakespeare's play.

clue.text: Actor with an E concession

blocks.note: first meaning: Richard E. ..., whose name carries the initial E
second meaning: something conceded or allowed

explanation.surface: An actor gets a discount marked E.
explanation.walkthrough: Concession reads as a cheap ticket; here it is simply a thing granted.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard E. Grant is a film actor, and a grant is something given or allowed, like a concession.

clue.text: Stop filming with a single light out

blocks.note: the director's call to stop the camera
and means together with
in cricket, a single is one run

explanation.surface: A film crew stops shooting when a lamp goes out.
explanation.walkthrough: Light out looks like a broken lamp on set, but it is the phrasal verb meaning to leave in a hurry.
explanation.definitionFit: To light out is informal for leaving quickly, and the idiom for abandoning something and fleeing fast is the same.

clue.text: Easy metal target

blocks.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
a shy is a target thrown at, as in a coconut shy

explanation.surface: A metal target is said to be easy to hit.
explanation.walkthrough: A coconut shy is a British fairground stall where you throw balls at coconuts.
explanation.definitionFit: Cushy is informal for easy and comfortable, as in a cushy job with little effort.

clue.text: Name the wheel-bound king: not I, Mr President

indicators.note: not means without, so one letter is taken away

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for name
in Greek myth King Ixion was bound to a fiery wheel by Zeus
taken as written, and removed

explanation.surface: A mythical king tied to a wheel protests that he is not the one, addressing the President.
explanation.walkthrough: Ixion has two I's; drop the second to leave IXON after N. Richard Nixon was the 37th US President.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Nixon was President of the United States, addressed formally as Mr President.

clue.text: Gives a leg up when society sits around

indicators.note: turned around, the following word's letters are moved into a new order

blocks.note: as can mean when
standard abbreviation for society
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone helps when polite society is sitting about idly.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone a leg up is to help them, which is what assisting someone means.

clue.text: Team turns to replace United in future match

indicators.note: turning round makes the team's numerals read the other way
to replace is to stand in for something, so one letter is swapped out

blocks.note: a football or cricket team has eleven players, XI in Roman numerals
U is the abbreviation for United in team names
taken as written

explanation.surface: A football team will take on Manchester United in a match to come.
explanation.walkthrough: United sounds like the club; it is only the letter U, the first one in the following word, that the reversed team replaces.
explanation.definitionFit: A fixture is a scheduled sporting match, a game fixed on the calendar.

clue.text: Lawrence Reagan's occupation

blocks.note: T. E. Lawrence, Lawrence of Arabia
Nancy Reagan, wife of President Ronald Reagan

explanation.surface: Lawrence Reagan is presented as an imagined person whose job is asked about.
explanation.walkthrough: Occupation looks like a job, but it means occupying a property.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenancy is the occupation of land or a building as a tenant, under a lease.

clue.text: Creating Disneyland ?- and not in old Lincolnshire

definitions.note: the answer was a division of old Lincolnshire, not the whole county

indicators.note: not means without, so that small word is taken away
creating something means making it anew out of the given material, so the letters are rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, and removed

explanation.surface: Someone imagines building a theme park in the English county of Lincolnshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Lincolnshire is an English county; it was historically split into three parts: Lindsey, Kesteven and Holland.
explanation.definitionFit: Lindsey was one of the three historic administrative parts of Lincolnshire, with Kesteven and Holland.
